description: Repainted by HARS to represent A7-076 and placed at RAAF Williamtown in October 2010 as a memorial to Flight Lieutenant Page and all No. 76 Squadron personnel who have died in service. Displayed at the base alongside the heritage centre.
aliases: MB326; MB326H; CA-30; CA30; Macchi; A7-076

description: Painted for the 50th anniversary of No. 76 Squadron and 25 years of RAAF Macchi operations but grounded for fatigue before it could fly the scheme; used as a travelling display and retains the commemorative markings.
Served with the Central Flying School and the Roulettes in 1970 and 1982, then 2 OCU and 77 and 76 Squadrons; painted with a red nose for Red Nose Day in 1991.
Ex-RAAF Winjeel, a training aid at RSTT Wagga before moving to Williamtown; on display since 26 June 2001.
Served with 79 Squadron at Ubon Thailand and 77 Squadron at Butterworth. Converted for display at the Base Squadron Williamtown entrance gate in 1971 and later moved inside the display hangar.

Displayed on a pole at Raymond Terrace NSW from 1981 to 2013 and badly deteriorated; removed in March 2013 and transported to Fighter World in February 2016. Repainted in a 79 Squadron scheme with a cobra on the tail.
The first Mirage fighter built in Australia, delivered 20 December 1963. Served with ARDU and 76 and 77 Squadrons at Williamtown; retired 31 March 1987 with 3580 hours.
aliases: Mirage IIIO; Mirage; Dassault Mirage III

description: Two-seat Mirage IIID trainer listed in survey inventories of Fighter World; the museum own page confirms a Mirage IIIO and IIID pair on display.
aliases: Mirage IIID; Mirage; Dassault Mirage III

description: Cockpit section only. Crashed at Williamtown on 6 March 1984 after an engine surge on finals, the pilot surviving; the remains became a training aid.
aliases: Mirage IIIO; Mirage; Dassault Mirage III

description: The first Australian-built Vampire. Instructional airframe No.16 at RSTT Wagga, transferred to Base Squadron Williamtown in February 1968 and displayed at the base main gate before moving into Fighter World.
Repainted in the South East Asia camouflage scheme after the F-111 retirement; departed Amberley on 4 May 2013 and arrived at Williamtown the following day.

Instructional airframe No.7 at RSTT Wagga from 1957, moved to Williamtown for display in April 1966 and shown at the base main gate. Restored by Fighter World in the chequered-tail markings of A77-881, the 77 Squadron formation display aircraft. The museum own webpage calls it A77-851, which is a different airframe whose cockpit is in South Australia.
Ex-Republic of Singapore Air Force Hunter carrying the number 546.

Wore mission markings for eight bombing sorties; upgraded to HUG Phase 2 and served with 3 and 75 Squadrons. Transferred to Air Force History and Heritage and displayed at the RAAF Base Williamtown Aviation Heritage Centre as Worimi.
Transferred to the Williamtown Aviation Heritage Centre in November 2019 for display as a PC-9/A(F) forward air control aircraft; on display from 17 March 2020.
Delivered to the Royal Australian Navy in December 1985 and formerly on outdoor display at the Jervis Bay Range Facility.
Full-scale non-flying replica of the Fokker triplane.
Full-scale non-flying replica displayed with the code D-X.
Full-scale non-flying replica displayed as A58-429/QY-V. Not a genuine airframe.
Full-scale non-flying replica; the museum own page lists Spitfire Mk VIII and Mk IX replicas.
Listed in survey inventories of Fighter World without an identity; understood to be a replica or reproduction rather than a wartime Messerschmitt.
Boeing Stearman listed on the museum own aircraft page; no registration published.
CT-4B Airtrainer listed on the museum own aircraft page; no serial published.
Bristol Bloodhound surface-to-air missile listed on the museum own aircraft page.
